extracted.intended_audience: students and problem-solvers of classical Euclidean geometry (high-school/undergraduate/contest training)
extracted.subtask_description: Working classical Euclidean geometry problems: constructions, loci, area/inequality arguments, and combinatorial/geometric reasoning using ruler-and-compass or paper-folding methods. The page gives problems and solution-principles used to produce/verify solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal areas for triangles with same base and altitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Two triangles with the same base and altitude have the same areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to equate triangle area expressions (Fig. 12.38) and to derive equalities among area-related segment sums; basic tool for area comparisons and reductions in many problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centroid/median stretching and area scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: The centroid divides medians in a 2:1 ratio; stretching (dilation) of a triangle about a vertex by factor k multiplies areas by k^2 and scales side lengths by k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection of the centroid at the midpoint and a dilation by factor 3 (example in solution 2) are used to construct related triangles with side lengths ma, mb, mc and to relate areas |ABC| = (3/4)|...| etc. Use centroid properties and area-scaling under dilation for constructive and area arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructibility condition for triangles with geometric-progression sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles with side lengths a, aq, aq^2 and aq, aq^2, aq^3 are similar and have two common sides; to be constructible they must satisfy the triangle inequality which imposes q-range: (√5 − 1)/2 < q < (√5 + 1)/2 (q ≠ 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the numeric constraint on common ratio q for existence of such triangles; examples: (1,3/2,9/4) and (3/2,9/4,27/8). Use triangle inequalities to check constructibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicular bisector by paper folding
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B coincide when folded, then every point X on the fold line satisfies |AX| = |BX|, so the fold is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction method: fold paper so A and B coincide; unfold and any point on the crease is equidistant from A and B. Useful ruler-free construction technique for perpendicular bisectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle with diameter as circumcircle of right triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle with diameter XY is the circumcircle of any right triangle having XY as hypotenuse (Thales' theorem consequence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in problem 7: circles with diameters AB, BC, CD, DA circumscribe the rectangular right triangles formed by dropping perpendiculars; used to detect right angles and cyclicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Altitude bound: h ≤ adjacent side and area bound |Δ| ≤ (base·adjacent_side)/2
rubrics_metrics.description: If a is the base and h the altitude of triangle ABC, and b one of the other sides, then h ≤ b. Hence area |ABC| ≤ ab/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to get upper bounds on areas and to derive equality conditions (e.g., equality when perpendicularity holds). Useful when bounding quadrilateral areas by summing triangle bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrilateral area upper bounds and equality conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadrilateral with ordered sides/adjacent sides a,b,c,d: |ABCD| ≤ (ab + cd)/2 (and other analogous bounds like |ABCD| ≤ (ac + bd)/2). Equality cases occur under orthogonality/cyclicity or for rectangles depending on arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use cutting along a diagonal, reflecting/turning triangles, and triangle-area bounds. Keep track of which sides are used as bases and when equality (rectangles, cyclic quadrilaterals) occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Median/median-point minimises sum of distances on a line (1D Fermat problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n points on a line x1 < x2 < ... < xn, the point P that minimizes the sum of distances ∑|xi − P| is: for odd n the median x_{(n+1)/2}; for even n any point in the interval [x_{n/2}, x_{n/2+1}] achieves the minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counting of points on each side of P to see slope changes of total-distance function. Extension to planar configurations: for some symmetric/convex cases the minimizer is a vertex or intersection of diagonals (see problem 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Location minimizing sum of distances to vertices in quadrilaterals (planar Fermat-like facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a quadrilateral is convex the point minimizing sum distances to the four vertices is the intersection O of the diagonals; if one vertex lies inside the triangle formed by the other three, that interior vertex minimizes the sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments use triangle inequalities and additivity; analyze cases by where vertices lie relative to convex hull. Useful when solving minimal-sum location problems in planar geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing sum of interior angles of star polygons via turning angle
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of interior angles of a star polygon can be found by walking around its contour with a pencil and adding vertex turns always in the same direction; this yields sums (e.g., star pentagon = 180°, S7,2 = 540°, S8,3 = 360°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This turning-angle method generalizes to nonconvex/star polygons and avoids piecemeal decomposition. Use consistent turning direction to obtain net rotation and hence sum of interior angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of sides vs altitudes: larger side ↔ smaller altitude
rubrics_metrics.description: If a ≤ b ≤ c (sides of triangle) then the corresponding altitudes satisfy hc ≤ hb ≤ ha. More generally, the sum la+lb+lc of distances from an interior point is bounded between the smallest and largest corresponding vertex altitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace side lengths cyclically in inequalities to relate altitudes and use monotonicity; the vertex with largest interior angle gives minimum of sum of distances, the one with smallest angle gives maximum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection-based midpoint inequality: |PM| ≤ (|PA| + |PB|)/2
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect point P at the midpoint M of AB to P'. Then |PM| ≤ (|PA| + |PB|)/2 (triangle inequality applied to reflected configuration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection to transform distance-sum problems into triangle side inequalities. Equality cases can be characterized (degenerate triangles etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference-of-distances inequality via midpoint reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: For reflection P' of P across midpoint M of AB, the sides of triangle AP'P are |PA|, |PB|, and 2|PM|. Hence ||PA| − |PB|| ≤ 2|PM| with equality for degenerate triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to bound difference of distances by twice distance to midpoint; apply when controlling how far a point can be from midpoints given side-distance differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of quadrilateral with fixed sides maximized when cyclic
rubrics_metrics.description: For a quadrilateral with given side lengths, the area as a function of one interior angle x satisfies F(x) = (ab/2) sin x + (cd/2) sin y with constraint relating x and y; maximizing area occurs when x + y = π, i.e., for a cyclic quadrilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate F(x) under the auxiliary constraint and deduce sign/critical point. Conclusion: among quadrilaterals with fixed side lengths the cyclic one maximizes area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of triangle type by side-length squares
rubrics_metrics.description: For triangle with sides a ≥ b ≥ c and opposite angle α to side a: α = 90° ⇔ a^2 = b^2 + c^2; α > 90° ⇔ a^2 > b^2 + c^2; α < 90° ⇔ a^2 < b^2 + c^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard cosine-law consequence; used as a test for obtuse/right/acute triangles and to derive contradictions in combinatorial geometric arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection (shadow) area maximized when object horizontal
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of the shadow (orthogonal projection) of a triangle onto a plane is maximized when the triangle is placed horizontal (maximizes projection onto table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric-optimal-placement principle: orient the figure to maximize projected area along given direction; applied to shadows or silhouette problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting triangles from points and interior points: x = 2m + n − 2
rubrics_metrics.description: If splitting an n-gon with m interior points into triangles, the number x of formed triangles satisfies x = 2m + n − 2 (or derive via Euler's formula f + v = e + 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods: direct angle-sum counting or Euler characteristic; useful when counting faces/triangles formed by diagonals and interior points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemmas for multi-colour-point configurations (existence of a four-colored plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: L1: If a straight line is three-colored then there exists a four-colored plane (take a point of the fourth color and any plane containing the line and that point). L2: If a three-colored plane and a line with the two other colors intersect, there exists a four-colored plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these lemmas to deduce global coloring conclusions from local color patterns; used in combinatorial geometry coloring proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of rectangle centers as circles (three-circle union)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a rectangle determined by fixed vertex pairs, as a chosen line a through A rotates, the locus of centers M of rectangles with fixed midpoints E,F is the circle with diameter EF; varying which opposite vertices lie on opposite sides gives the union of three such circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction technique: vary a parameter and trace locus via circle constructions with diameters determined by midpoints; useful for locus/construction problems involving centers of rectangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of midpoints for two circles (rolling circle midpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix X on circle C1; as Y traces circle C2 the midpoint XY traces a circle of radius r2/2 about midpoint of XO2; letting X vary over C1 the union is an annular region with inner radius (r1 − r2)/2 and outer radius (r1 + r2)/2 centered at midpoint of O1O2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a geometric description of midpoints of corresponding points on two circles; practical for locus problems involving midpoints and rolling circles.
